items.title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
items.description:
arXiv:2611.17563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a sho
items.summary: A study published on arXiv demonstrates that when language models face self-disagreement or counter-reasoning, benchmarks fail to accurately reflect real-world deployment scenarios where answers are often contested. This highlights the need for more robust testing methods that account for model uncertainty and debate.
items.summary_detailed: The research presented in the arXiv paper "Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement" demonstrates that language models often fail when faced with self-disagreement or counter-reasoning, as they are typically evaluated through benchmarks that present questions without contestation. This finding highlights a gap between model performance in isolation and their real-world deployment where answers can be challenged. The broader impact suggests the need for more robust testing methods that simulate the dynamic nature of human interaction to better prepare language models for practical use.
items.summary_bullets:
• Benchmarks often measure language models in isolation.
• Deployment scenarios involve contestation of model answers.
• Models can provide incorrect answers when challenged logically.
• The failure highlights issues beyond the scope of current benchmarks.
